analysis.one_liner: Requires security inspection of all cargo carried aboard passenger airplanes.
analysis.headline: The bill to inspect all cargo on passenger planes was referred to a House subcommittee and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 9/11 attacks, checked passenger baggage had to be screened for explosives, but cargo packed onto the same passenger planes generally was not. This bill would have directed the Department of Homeland Security to build a system inspecting every piece of cargo on passenger aircraft, ramping up to one-third of cargo screened within a year, two-thirds within two years, and all of it within three years, using the same standards as passenger baggage screening.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers — including the crews flying those planes — get the assurance that the hold beneath them is checked for explosives to the same standard as their own checked bags.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Passengers and crews on passenger planes

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Secretary of Homeland Security to establish a system to inspect all cargo transported on passenger aircraft, for both U.S. and foreign carriers.
Requires screening equipment, technology, and personnel to meet the same standards already established for inspecting passenger baggage.
Phases in coverage on a fixed schedule: one-third of cargo inspected by the first Thanksgiving after enactment, two-thirds by the second, and all cargo by the third.

analysis.who_pays: Airlines and air cargo companies would bear the cost of screening every piece of belly cargo — equipment, personnel, and delays — and the bill contains no funding provision, so taxpayers could also share the bill through DHS appropriations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Passenger airlines and air cargo carriers

drawbacks.text: The bill sets a hard screening mandate but provides no dedicated funding, leaving airlines and DHS to absorb the cost of equipment and personnel to baggage-screening standards.

Applying passenger-baggage screening standards to freight of all shapes and sizes is technically demanding; a fixed three-year timetable could strain available explosive-detection capacity and add shipping costs that get passed into airfares and freight prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The security gap the bill addressed was real: millions of pounds of freight flew under passengers without the screening their own bags received. The cost of closing it falls on a concentrated industry and partly on taxpayers, and the bill's rigid Thanksgiving deadline left little room for phased technology deployment. Still, a full vote would have forced Congress to weigh that trade-off explicitly — which never happened.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Homeland Security Committee, which passed it down to a subcommittee, where it sat with no further action until that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Markey introduced the bill on November 17, 2005, joined by Rep. Christopher Shays, and it was referred to the House Committee on Homeland Security.
Twelve days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Economic Security, Infrastructure Protection, and Cybersecurity, and no further action was taken for the rest of the 109th Congress.
The bill attracted four cosponsors, two Republicans and two Democrats, but never received a markup, floor vote, or hearing in the record shown.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Passenger airlines and air cargo carriers came out ahead, since the screening mandate never took effect and they avoided its costs; passengers kept flying over unscreened cargo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Airlines and cargo carriers avoided screening costs

for.name: Rep. Edward J. Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Safe Skies Cargo Inspection Act to require inspection of all cargo on passenger aircraft.

for.name: Rep. Christopher Shays
for.what_they_did: Joined Markey in introducing the bill at its filing.

for.name: 4 cosponsors (2 Republicans, 2 Democrats)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors after introduction.

against.name: House Homeland Security Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and referred it to the Subcommittee on Economic Security, Infrastructure Protection, and Cybersecurity, where it remained without action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was led by a Democrat and a Republican together and drew cosponsors from both parties; no recorded opposition vote ever occurred because it never reached the floor.

industries.note: Airlines would have had to screen all belly cargo to baggage standards, adding equipment and labor costs, though uniform rules would apply to U.S. and foreign carriers alike. The bill's death spared them those costs.
Shippers moving freight on passenger planes would face inspection delays and fees; blocking the mandate kept their low-cost access to passenger aircraft holds intact.

industries.industry: Explosive-detection equipment and screening technology makers
industries.note: A mandate to screen 100% of passenger-aircraft cargo to baggage standards would have created a large new market for detection equipment and screening services.
